title: Chapter 17 — The Luxury Customer & How Luxury Selling Differs
intro: Who buys luxury appliances, what they are actually buying, and the posture the tier demands.

sections.title: The Luxury Customer Profile
sections.content:
The luxury appliance customer — $10K-plus kitchen packages, Sub-Zero, Wolf, Miele, Gaggenau, La Cornue — is a fundamentally different sale. Price is not the objection. Being ignored or talked down to is.

They have already done research. They know what they want or think they do. They are investing in their home, not buying an appliance. They want expertise, not enthusiasm. Calm confidence beats excited pitching. They value their time above all else — be efficient, not wordy. They often have a designer or architect involved. Respect the team.

sections.title: How to Sell Luxury
sections.content:
The conversation should happen in a quiet area. Not yelling over the floor noise. If you have a design center or a separate area, use it.

Listen more. The luxury customer will tell you exactly what they want if you let them talk. Your job is to refine, not redirect.

Tell the craft story. 'Wolf ranges are built in a single factory in Wisconsin. Each range takes about three hours to assemble by hand. The infrared broiler is exclusive to Wolf — no other residential brand has one.' Craft, heritage, and exclusivity sell at this level.

Do not apologize for the price. Never say 'I know it is expensive.' Say 'This is a lifetime investment in your kitchen. The resale value alone typically pays for itself.'

sections.title: The Luxury Package
sections.content:
Luxury customers rarely buy one piece. 'Since we are doing Wolf for cooking, have you considered the Sub-Zero column refrigeration? The panel-ready design gives you a fully integrated kitchen — everything disappears behind your cabinetry.'

At this tier, delivery is an experience, not a transaction. Coordinate installation timing, protect the home, and follow up personally.

The luxury close is usually quieter than a standard close. 'I will put this together for you. Should I send the specs to your designer, or would you prefer to handle that?'

sections.title: Loss Aversion at Scale
sections.content:
The deeper truth about luxury selling: loss aversion scales with the ticket. A customer spending $25,000 on a kitchen is not excited — they are terrified of making the wrong choice. Their deepest need is usually certainty that the choice is right.

Your job is to reduce their anxiety, not increase their excitement. Provide evidence. Reference other installations you have done at this tier. Show them reviews from similar projects. Connect them with your designer for a second opinion.

The luxury customer who feels rushed will walk. The one who feels guided will buy everything you recommend.
